list.listitem: Grades I-III vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) resolve spontaneously at a rate of about 13% per year in the first 5 years and 3.5% per year thereafter; Grades IV-V VUR have a 5% yearly rate of resolution.
Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG), renal ultrasound, and Dimercapto-succinic acid (DMSA) scan may be used in select patients in follow-up after a febrile UTI but is unlikely to change management.C

Prophylactic antibiotic therapy in VUR reduces the likelihood of recurrent UTI and AUA guidelines recommend it for children with who are 1 year or older and have a history of bowel/bladder dysfunction, recurrent febrile UTI or renal cortical scarring. B
Prophylactic antibiotic therapy in VUR reduces the risk of recurrence but not of renal scarring.A
Surgery for VUR is increasingly not recommended and should be addressed on a case-by-case basis.C

background.definition: The American Urological Association defines vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) as retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the upper urinary tract. See for definitions of VUR grades I to V.

list.listitem: There are approximately seven hospitalizations for VUR per 100,000 children per year.

VUR is more common than previously thought but is often asymptomatic; it is present in 17% of children without UTI and 31% with UTI. In one study, 96% of VUR found during evaluation of children with UTI was low grade (I-III).
In 2000, total expenditures for inpatient treatment of pediatric VUR were $47 million, an increase of more than $10 million since 1997.
Primary VUR is caused by a congenital anomaly of the ureterovesical junction, leading to retrograde flow of urine to the upper urinary tract.
Secondary VUR is a result of increased intravesical pressure associated with anatomic obstruction (posterior urethral valves) or functional obstruction (spina bifida or neurogenic bladder).
VUR predisposes patients to acute pyelonephritis by transporting bacteria from the bladder to the kidney.
Late stage complications include renal scarring (reflux nephropathy).
Extensive scarring may progress to hypertension (secondary) secondary hypertension, decreased renal function, proteinuria and even chronic renal failure end-stage renal disease.
It is unclear how often pediatric UTI results in renal failure.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Younger age at diagnosis of UTI

list.listitem: While evidence supporting screening for VUR is lacking, children who have parents or siblings diagnosed with VUR may be considered for screening VCUG. C
Infants and children presenting with unexplained fever of 38ºC or higher should have a urine sample tested after 24 hours at the latest.
VCUG, renal ultrasound, and DMSA scan may be used in selected patients in follow-up after a febrile UTI, but are unlikely to change management.C

If hydronephrosis is observed on prenatal ultrasound, 40% of infants have VUR. An ultrasound should be performed after birth to further assess this and some experts recommend a full evaluation including VCUG although clinical trials are lacking. C
VUR is common in children with first UTI, but the clinical significance of this finding is unclear.
Suspect VUR in infants with prenatal hydronephrosis and when there is a family history of VUR in parents or siblings.
VCUG is the gold standard for the diagnosis of VUR.

Renal ultrasonography is useful in assessing kidney size and medical renal disease or scarring. DMSA scintigraphy is used to detect and follow progression of renal scarring. These tests are of limited value in most patients.

Using specific renal ultrasound criteria of hydroureter, duplication and renal dysmorphia for patients with prenatal hydronephrosis can help to risk stratify patients more likely to need VCUG to detect VUR.

A renal ultrasound within 6 weeks is recommended for children under 6 months of age after a first UTI. Ultrasound of the urinary tract after a first UTI has poor sensitivity, but is recommended by the AAP after an initial urinary tract infection. However, a recent study of the cost-effectiveness of routine, screening renal bladder ultrasound (RBUS) for a first, febrile UTI in children age 2-24 months does not meet cost-effectiveness guidelines and should be deferred until a second UTI.

For children 2 years of age or less who have a febrile UTI, an acute DMSA scan may be valuable in the exclusion of dilating VUR; since the presence of VUR on VCUG is rather low when DMSA is negative, a DMSA may be considered to assess the need for a VCUG.

Approximately 5% of children with UTI will have an abnormal DMSA examination, but the clinical utility and long-term significance of this finding is unclear. A DMSA scan may be considered after an abnormal ultrasound or in follow-up after atypical or recurrent UTI.
A child with a normal DMSA scan has less than a 1% chance of having high grade VUR. However, routine use of DMSA scans will lead to many false positive tests. Usefullness of this test is uncertain.
No high quality studies directly assess the benefit of using VCUG routinely in children with UTI.

The use of VCUG after first UTI is recommended by one guideline only for children less than 6 months old with atypical UTI or recurrent UTI. The American Academy of Pediatrics only recommends a VCUG after a first UTI if an ultrasound is abnormal and suggests high grade VUR. However, imaging is unlikely to change management after a first UTI.
Conscious sedation with midazolam, psychological preparation, and warmed contrast media are all options to reduce pain and distress with VCUG.

Prophylactic antibiotic therapy in VUR reduces the likelihood of recurrent UTI and AUA guidelines recommend it for children with who are 1 year or older and have a history of bowel/bladder dysfunction, recurrent febrile UTI or renal cortical scarring. B
Surgery for VUR is increasingly not recommended and should be considered on a case-by-case basis. C

Evidence is mixed on the benefit of antibiotic prophylaxis in children with VUR. Prophylaxis does not change the likelihood of renal scarring, at least over the medium term, and may increase infectious and infections caused by resistant organisms.

American Urological Association guidelines updated in 2017 recommend antibiotic prophylaxis for children less than 1 year of age based on expert opinion. They performed meta-analysis of 7 trials and concluded that there was a significant reduction in the likelihood of recurrent UTI with prophylaxis, which was numerically greater in non-dilated cases than in dilated cases. However, studies were quite heterogeneous and the more appropriate random effects meta-analysis did not find a statistically significant reduction in the risk of recurrent UTI for non-dilated (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.35-1.14) or dilated cases (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.56-1.08). The AUA guidelines recommend prophylaxis for children over one year of age with bladder/bowel dysfunction, recurrent febrile UTI or renal cortical abnormalities, while for children without those problems observation is a reasonable option.
Antibiotic regimens include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (1-2 mg/kg/day of TMP component), trimethoprim alone (1-2 mg/kg/day), and nitrofurantoin (1-2 mg/kg/day).

A recent multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled study of 607 children with VUR diagnosed after symptomatic UTI did not support routine monitoring of electrolyte, renal or hematologic laboratory tests in children receiving long-term TMP-SMZ prophylaxis.

Antibiotic prophylaxis prevents a first UTI in children with Grade III to V VUR (NNT=7) but has no impact on renal outcomes. Girls and patients with a prior infection are more likely to benefit. The harm-benefit ratio for antibiotics should be carefully considered.
Long term risks of medical therapy include nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, increased antibiotic resistance, and rarely serious reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or marrow suppression.
Open surgical reimplantation of ureters has correction rate of 93% to 99%.
Subureteric transurethral injection (STING procedure) involves injection of copolymer beneath the mucosa of the UV junction via cystoscope. It has a correction rate of 75% to 85%.
Both surgical procedures have the risk of ureteral obstruction; less than 0.7% for STING procedure and 6.6% for reimplantation surgery.
Eight children would need to be treated with surgical correction to prevent one episode of febrile UTI over the next 5 years with no change in risk of renal scarring (NNT = 8).
Surgical repair is an option according to one guideline, most recently updated in 2017, but is not recommended by another.

Since VUR in infancy often resolves or improves spontaneously, surgery should be directed toward patients unlikely to experience resolution, i.e., those with an abnormal initial DMSA scan, Grade V disease or breakthrough febrile UTIs.
Laparascopic and robot assisted laparascopic surgeries may be an option if surgical re-implantation is planned.
Patients with dysfunctional voiding and VUR may benefit from therapy directed at improving voiding patterns with bladder training.
Oxybutynin enhances hydronephrosis improvement and vesicoureteral reflux resolution following primary endoscopic valve ablation in infants but periodic monitoring is warranted.
Patients with VUR, especially higher grades, should be referred to pediatric urologists or nephrologists for evaluation.
Grades I-III VUR resolve spontaneously at a rate of about 13% per year in the first 5 years and 3.5% per year thereafter; Grades IV to V VUR have a 5% yearly rate of resolution. B
One algorithm for timing of follow-up VCUG suggests every 2 years for Grades I to II and every 3 years for Grades III to V. B
Non-white race, mild grade VUR, absence of renal damage and absence of dysfunctional voiding are all independent predictors of VUR resolution. B
Late stage complications of reflux nephropathy may include hypertension (38%), proteinuria (31%), renal insufficiency (24%), UTIs (15%), and urinary calculi (6%). B
More than half of pregnant women with VUR experience complications during pregnancy.
Physiologic dilation of the urinary tract and increased GFR predispose those with VUR to UTI, eclampsia, and progression of renal disease.

tr.td: Reflux into ureter, renal pelvis, and renal calyces but no dilation and normal calyceal fornices
Mild or moderate ureteral dilation, tortuosity, or both, as well as mild or moderate dilation of the renal pelvis
Moderate ureteral dilation, tortuosity, or both, as well as moderate dilation of the renal pelvis and calcyces
Gross ureteral dilation and tortuosity, as well as gross dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces
